top.description: Nov 11, 2026; Houston, Texas, USA; Golden State Warriors guard Stephen Curry (30) holds his side during the first quarter against the Houston Rockets at Toyota Center. Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images Stephen Curry will not return for the rest of the game tonight after exiting the game less than six minutes into the first quarter of the Warriors’ matchup against the Rockets in Houston. Curry initially got tangled up with Alperen Sengun less than four minutes into the game when he was first spotted grabbing the right side of his abdomen. Minutes later, the 38-year-old veteran grimaced in pain after hitting a three-pointer. He immediately turned around, realized something was wrong, yelled in frustration, and the team called a timeout. Stephen Curry headed to the locker room with an apparent right hip injury. — ESPN (@espn) November 12, 2026 Curry headed straight for the locker room, followed by the Warriors’ director of medical services, Drew Yoder. Later, Anthony Slater, ESPN’s insider for the Warriors, reported that Curry would not return for the rest of the game because he was out with right abdominal soreness. NBA fans held their breath in disbelief as they saw this incident and read the update on social media. They flooded social media with dejected reactions. “If he doesn’t come back, we are about to go on a losing streak… Houston plays too aggressively.” “Hoping this is nothing serious. 🙏 The Warriors can’t afford to lose Steph Curry to another injury. Get well soon, Chef! ❤️🏀” “Oh my God, man! 💔💔💔💔💔💔” “Never a good sight. Hoping it’s nothing serious. 💔” “God f–king damn it, every time we play the Rockets.” This is a major setback for the Warriors, who need Stephen Curry to be healthy to contend realistically. Ahead of tonight’s game, he was averaging 30.6 points, 4.1 rebounds, and 4.3 assists per game while shooting 50.3% from the field and 45.7% from behind the three-point line. It is unfortunate that just two games ago, Stephen Curry said that as long as he’s healthy, he’ll keep giving it his all for the Warriors after a 41-point masterclass. Several fans unfairly blamed Amen Thompson for the injury, since he was Curry’s primary defender tonight. Driven by viral pregame comments from Ime Udoka, who said Amen Thompson was the Rockets’ only solution to stop Stephen Curry tonight, many of them clearly didn’t watch the game, since Thompson didn’t touch his abdomen at all on the play where the soreness seemed to worsen. They also seem to have missed the play a few minutes before the shot where Curry’s discomfort seemingly began. Nonetheless, we hope this does not lead to an extended absence for the veteran superstar. The Warriors will now wait for more information on Curry’s health, hoping the pain in his abdomen won’t worsen. Any prolonged absence could significantly affect their performance because the veteran superstar carries much of their offensive load this season. top.description: LAS VEGAS – Triston Casas will play for Tigres del Licey of the Dominican Winter League this offseason. The 26-year-old first baseman also played for Licey during the 2022-23 offseason. “I don’t have a definitive date,” said president of baseball operations Craig Breslow. “Still needs to ramp up in terms of game speed and intensity. But he is feeling good, so we’re optimistic he’s gonna be able to compete in Winter League games.” Casas has not played in a major league game since rupturing his left patellar tendon more than 18 months ago on May 2, 2025. He dealt with a left-side intercostal strain earlier in the 2026 season, then underwent arthroscopic wrist surgery in August. “He’s obviously missed a significant amount of time over the last couple of years so we don’t have real workload concerns in terms of total volume,” Breslow said. “We just want to make sure that his body is ready to do what will be asked of it and what’s required of playing in a pretty competitive environment.” Whitlock’s leg injury was a stress fracture As previously reported, imaging revealed that setup man Garrett Whitlock pitched through a fractured tibia late in the 2026 season. top.title: Rutgers women's basketball wins but major scare from Monmouth, Gigi Gamble
top.description: PISCATAWAY -- The Rutgers women's basketball team avoided an upset Wednesday night when the Scarlet Knights came back from 17-point deficit to defeat Monmouth University 64-62. With the game tied 62-62, Mia Pauldo got the ball off the screen, drove right, stopped and hit a midrange jumper to give Rutgers the lead with 3.4 seconds left. The possession before, Pauldo hit a floater in the paint to get the lead before Monmouth's Gigi Gamble tied it up with free throws. More: Rutgers women's basketball has Hope. Masonius comes home for new beginning | Exclusive Monmouth led by as much as 17 points but the game was tied after Rutgers went on an 18-6 run in the third quarter. "Honestly, we had this game," said Monmouth's Gigi Gamble, who had a game-high 30 was named the Coastal Athletic Conference Preseason Player of the Year. "We had it, it hurts, but it should give us more fuel, more fight, more hunger, more heart." "We're going to keep building off it. So I'm not worried about this loss." Rutgers is 4-0 but this was by far the closest call the Big Ten team has had. "Coach (Gary Redus) had a talk while I was on the bench and he said the best players aren't who they are when things are only going good for them, they're who they are when things are going bad for them," said Pauldo, who scored 7 points in the first half but finished with a team-high 17. "I took that in and was like, yeah I want to be the best player and I was messing up in the first half and I wasn't focused enough. And I was like to take responsibility in this game, if we really want to win this game I got to lock in and step up and be the best player." Monmouth got a chance to tie with 3.0 seconds left but turned the ball over on the inbounds to seal the win for the Scarlet Knights. The Scarlet Knights (4-0) came out the gate slow but picked up the defensive pressure in the second half to hold off a Monmouth (2-1) team that's projected to win the Coastal Athletic Association Conference. So far this season, Rutgers has faced mid-majors and Tuesday was no different, but the level of pressure was different. Redus labeled the game a "wake up call." "I would've liked us to be a little bit more aggressive tonight," Redus said. "I felt like we could've come out and we could've had more aggression especially on the defensive end. I didn't like our defensive effort at all in the first half. That was the issue. We had nine points in the first quarter but the offense is gonna be hit or miss at times with any team. Especially in close games, it's your defense that has to carry you." They shot 55% in the first half so that's what I told them, it was the defense." One of the biggest bright spots for Rutgers was the way it was able share the ball. Eight different Scarlet Knights were able to score the ball on Wednesday which came in handy. Especially in the third quarter when Rutgers went on a 18-2 run to go into the last quarter tied 44-44. Rutgers first lead came with 9:28 left in the last quarter

top.title: Ford Veterans Day Classic at Daytona is a hit. Will it return? If so, where?
top.description: Yes, we can call it the “inaugural” Veterans Day Classic at Daytona. We’ll eventually see the TV numbers from USA Network’s Wednesday night coverage. But the eyeball test suggests a hit for the Ford Motor Company, its Ford Racing division, and the combo of NASCAR and Daytona International Speedway. “We love throwing races. We love throwing big events. We love partnering with friends like Ford,” Speedway President Frank Kelleher said Wednesday night while mixing in the thick FanZone crowd. Logistics can be, you know, logistical, and sometimes timing and schedules are a challenge, but Veterans Day appears to fall in a unique place on the calendar — right after the NASCAR season, just before the holidays start dominating the scene. Thankfully, Veterans Day isn’t going anywhere, and my guess is Ford will always have cars to sell, so maybe this becomes a yearly thing. “I would love it,” Kelleher said. “We know how to execute high-level music acts. Music and racing are definitely in our DNA.” Except he then tossed in a wrinkle worth noting. “We will be excited to chat with Ford and everyone involved in the weeks to come and see if it makes sense to bring it back, whether it be here at Daytona International Speedway or perhaps at another speedway.” Will Veterans Day Classic return? Probably. But where? … Or perhaps at another Speedway. That seems like a logical move. However, and back to logistics, Wednesday’s event had the advantage of blending into an existing Daytona race week — Historic Sportscar Racing’s 12th annual Daytona Classic 24, which started Wednesday and runs through Sunday. The track’s race operations were already in place, which brings a nice advantage. We’re LIVE from Daytona for the Veterans Day Classic! 🇺🇸🏁 📺 : USA Netwok pic.twitter.com/cZOeXCYmIm — NASCAR on USA (@NASCARonUSA) November 12, 2026 Given the HSR presence, the garage area was wall-to-wall with a wide variety of yesterday’s racing machinery, including cars that previously ran here in both stock-car and sportscar races. For anyone who walked the grounds and saw the recent racing equipment and virtual museum pieces, there was contrast, since one of two threads running through it all was promotion of Ford’s new Mustang Dark Horse. The NASCAR version of the new Mustang was unveiled Wednesday afternoon at the museum outside Turn 4. The road-racing version was center stage for the 30-minute race on Daytona’s Rolex 24 road course. The other thread, of course, was Veterans Day. The Speedway and NASCAR have always leaned heavily toward the promotion of our nation’s military and its veterans. Usually, it’s part of the show. Wednesday, that theme blanketed the entire evening of loud music and louder machines. And you’d have a hard time finding anything other than a thumbs-up from those who joined the festivities. top.title: Austin Reaves injured as Lakers win seventh in a row
top.description: Austin Reaves drives to the basket against Milwaukee's Ryan Rollins in the first half. (Aaron Gash / Associated Press) The Lakers won their seventh straight game. They could lose something bigger. Star guard Austin Reaves left Wednesday’s 123-112 win over the Milwaukee Bucks with a left heel injury and did not return. Reaves, who scored 18 points with five assists and three steals, landed awkwardly on a blocked dunk attempt during the third quarter but stayed in the game despite appearing to be in discomfort on the bench during an ensuing timeout. He covered his head with a towel on the sideline, but played three more minutes until he eventually subbed himself out during live play. After center Walker Kessler grabbed a defensive rebound, Reaves staggered to the bench and limped toward the tunnel, forcing the Lakers to call a time out with 5:20 remaining in the third. top.title: Revived Fuellkrug relishes home comforts on Germany return
top.description: Niclas Fuellkrug (R) has been in top form since returning to Werder Bremen (Kirill KUDRYAVTSEV) After ill-fated stints at West Ham and AC Milan, striker Niclas Fuellkrug's rich vein of form since his Werder Bremen return has been capped with a Germany recall. Germany coach Jurgen Klopp brought Fuellkrug back into the fold for Nations League fixtures against Serbia on Friday and the Netherlands next week. Fuellkrug has not played an international game since a Nations League third-place playoff loss to France in June 2025. While Klopp, who has a contract until after the 2030 World Cup, has stated his focus is on youth and building for the future, Fuellkrug made himself impossible to ignore. Currently the Bundesliga's top scorer ahead of Harry Kane, the 33-year-old has 12 goals in 11 matches in all competitions, having managed only four in two seasons after leaving Germany for West Ham. Klopp admitted "sometimes form trumps everything else". "He made his case with a wide variety of goals... and almost all of them were spectacular," said Klopp. Fuellkrug also has an excellent record for Germany with 14 goals in just 24 appearances, many of which came as a substitute. Fuellkrug has a simple explanation for his form since returning to Bremen on a season-long loan from now-Championship side West Ham. "It's my footballing home," Fuellkrug said of the club he first joined aged 14. "Everyone sleeps better in their own bed. I just feel completely at ease here." Fuellkrug became the latest striker to endure an unhappy time at West Ham, a club which has become a graveyard for promising European forwards. He scored just three times in an injury-hit 18 months in London. But while he may not have gotten among the goals, his endeared himself to some of the fanbase with his typically German honesty. After conceding late to draw 1-1 at home to Southampton in April 2025, Fuellkrug spoke his mind, using a swear word to describe the Hammers' performance, with the West Ham fans then using his quote to create a chant referencing him. Fuellkrug's honesty has also won him support among many in Germany, where the gap-toothed journeyman is seen as an antidote to the modern image-conscious footballer. "I couldn't stay fit," Fuellkrug said of his struggles abroad, adding: "The key is staying fit and having a team around me that looks for me -- and passes me the ball when the moment is right. "That's the key -- I think I've been able to prove that now." - Klose an 'inspiration' - Fuellkrug is in blistering form but his call-up highlights how bare the cupboard now is in a country once known for producing top-class forwards. The four-time world champions have produced strikers like Gerd Mueller, Fritz Walter, Ulf Kirsten, Rudi Voeller and Jurgen Klinsmann. But Germany have not had a top-class number nine since 2014 World Cup-winner Miroslav Klose. Of Germany's current generation, Kai Havertz regularly starts up front but the Arsenal man has never been an out-and-out goalscorer.

top.title: Deshaun Watson makes feelings clear on Texans reunion as DeMeco Ryans delivers verdict
top.description: Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images Deshaun Watson has played down the significance of facing his former team as the Cleveland Browns prepare to take on the Houston Texans in Week 10. The quarterback will meet Houston for just the second time since being traded to Cleveland, having previously spent the first four seasons of his NFL career with the franchise that drafted him 12th overall in 2017. However, Watson insists his attention is firmly on helping the Browns return to winning ways and remain in the playoff hunt. DeMeco Ryans praises Deshaun Watson ahead of Houston Texans reunion Speaking to reporters, Watson made it clear that the personal storyline surrounding the reunion was no longer important to him. “It’s a big opportunity for us. Get back on the winning track, especially get in front of our home fans. That’s the ultimate focus, is focus on that. All the outside things, going against my former team, that stuff was in the past. Four, five years ago? Yeah, it was a big deal,” Watson said. “Now, I think both sides have moved on, and we’re just both trying to find ways to win and continue to put ourselves in position for later on down the road.” Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans also had plenty of praise for Watson, highlighting his decision-making and ability to escape pressure. “I’ve seen a guy who’s being very decisive with the football. He’s getting the ball out of his hands very quickly. When it’s not there, it’s his athletic ability to escape the pocket,” Ryans said. He also pointed to Watson’s performances in important moments, adding: “The thing that showed up the most for me watching the Browns throughout this year is how they performed in those clutch moments and those two-minute moments situations. top.description: SUNBURY, Ohio – Teddy Peterson rejoined the Wyoming High School soccer program this season after focusing on football for the past two years. The Wyoming junior goalkeeper, who has a lot of experience in net in club ball, made the biggest save of his career. nigeria.description: Last week, I started a discussion of General Yakubu Gowon’s multi-themed memoirs, My Life of Duty & Allegiance. My focus was on the book’s general tone, which I find unduly self-justificatory. In his attempts to defend his legacy, General Gowon presents himself as a saintly figure who did no wrong as a leader, whereas some introspection and nuanced reflection would have helped. That said, the book is a treasure trove of insightful details that enrich our historical narrative. This week, I will focus on one of such insights, namely, the quality of governance and public service ethos under General Gowon’s regime, with Chief Obafemi Awolowo singled out as the arrowhead of a remarkable governance approach that, if replicated today, would transform how Nigeria is governed and, thus, this country’s fortunes. As a political economist and policy practitioner who spent nearly 20 years advising the UK government on diverse policy areas, in addition to teaching public policy, I have professional and intellectual interests in how government is run. Thus, I was enthralled by General Gowon’s fascinating accounts of how the affairs of state were conducted under his administration, with the triumvirate of politicians (as ministers), civil servants (as technocrats), and universities and think-tanks (as sounding boards) driving policy formulation and implementation and setting standards of good and effective governance. Sitting atop the triumvirate was Chief Awolowo, an extraordinarily transformative leader! Indeed, if General Gowon’s memoirs can be said to have a hero, that hero is Chief Obafemi Awolowo, appointed by Gowon as the Vice Chairman of the Federal Executive Council, FEC, and Commissioner of Finance in his administration. nigeria.title: The US built world’s greatest card system
nigeria.description: By YVONNE-FAITH ELAIGWU The history of payments is, in many ways, the history of making value easier to move. We started at barter and are now at electronic transfers, with stablecoins suggesting that the next evolution is here. New payment methods rarely make their predecessors useless. Cash did not immediately eliminate barter. Cards did not eliminate cheques. Account-to-account payments will not eliminate cards. But payments evolve. And one of the most interesting examples of that evolution can be found in an unlikely comparison: Nigeria and the United States. The United States built perhaps the world’s greatest card ecosystem. Nigeria just seems to have built past it. The American card system is extraordinary. Over decades, the U.S. built an ecosystem connecting consumers, merchants, issuing banks, acquiring banks, and card networks. Around it grew credit bureaus, credit scores, revolving credit, chargebacks, fraud protection, loyalty points, airline miles, and billions of dollars of rewards. Consequently, Americans have a compelling reason to use cards. And use them, they do. Data from the Federal Reserve show that credit-card payments reached 67.1 billion transactions in 2024, while ACH processed an enormous $104.06 trillion in 2024. America, therefore, doesn’t lack account-to-account infrastructure. The difference is where A2A sits in everyday consumer behaviour. Walk into an American store, and the natural question is still: Which card am I using? In Nigeria, increasingly, a different question is asked: “What is your account number?” That difference is more significant than it appears. Nigeria took another road. Nigeria never developed America’s deep credit-card culture. Debit cards became widespread, but cards did not become as deeply embedded in the country’s economic architecture as they did in America. Instead, Nigeria increasingly solved digital payments at the bank-account level. At the centre of this transformation is the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System and its NIBSS Instant Payment platform, built to operate 24/7 with most transactions settling in under one second. This infrastructure changed behaviour. Any individual or company can pay another individual or merchant, and the transaction can be executed on a Friday evening or a Sunday morning. The expectation is still remarkably simple: the money should arrive now. That expectation is one of Nigeria’s greatest payment achievements. America’s success may be part of its problem. This is where the comparison becomes fascinating. America isn’t stuck on cards because it cannot build something better. It may be stuck on cards partly because cards work so well. The merchant already has the terminal. The consumer already has the card. The bank earns card revenue. Visa and Mastercard provide enormous networks. nigeria.title: 2027 Elections: Beyond INEC, 375 Judges’ integrity under trial
nigeria.description: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri With the 2027 general elections just 65 days away, all eyes are on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to conduct a smooth, free, fair, and credible poll. Meanwhile, preparations for the aftermath are already under way. A total of 375 judges have been nominated to serve on election petition tribunals, where they will adjudicate disputes brought by candidates and parties dissatisfied with the results. The judges, drawn from courts across the federation, were inaugurated on Monday, November 9, at a ceremony held at the Body of Benchers Complex in Abuja. Section 285(1) and (2) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, vests in the President of the Court of Appeal the responsibility for constituting election petition tribunals to adjudicate disputes arising from National and State Houses of Assembly and governorship elections. Similarly, section 134(3)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026, prescribes the timelines for constituting the tribunals and opening their registries. The swearing-in, organised by the President of the Court of Appeal, Justice Monica Dongban-Mensem, marked the formal assumption of a responsibility with considerable constitutional, professional and public significance. A three-day intensive workshop followed immediately. It was designed to deepen the judges’ knowledge of the Electoral Act 2026, familiarise them with applicable practice directions and the evolving jurisprudence of the courts on election-related cases, and sharpen the practical skills needed for case management, evaluation of evidence, control of proceedings, and the delivery of clear, well-reasoned judgments within the prescribed timelines. The CJN also used the occasion to launch the second edition of the Judicial Electoral Manual (JEM), which she said will help judicial officers locate relevant authorities, appreciate the development of the law and approach recurring issues with greater clarity. According to the CJN, by bringing together the relevant constitutional provisions, the Electoral Act 2026, applicable practice directions and judicial decisions, the Manual provides a useful resource for judicial officers and other stakeholders in the electoral adjudicatory process. She was quick to warn, however, that it should serve only as a guide and a reference tool. It does not replace independent judicial reasoning or relieve any judicial officer of the duty to consider each case on its own facts, the arguments of counsel and the applicable law. The Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Prince Lateef Fagbemi, SAN, said the early swearing-in of the tribunal judges was a clear demonstration of the judiciary’s commitment to ensuring that electoral disputes are handled promptly, competently and in accordance with the law. nigeria.title: Gbenga Omotoso at 65: A rare gift of generosity and mentorship
nigeria.description: By ROBERT UWEMEDIMO When Debbi Fields observed that “there is no such thing as coincidence; people come into our lives for a reason,” she captured a truth I have come to know profoundly through my relationship with Mr. Gbenga Omotoso. As he turned 65 on November 11, 2026, I pause to reflect on the extraordinary journey of more than two decades I have been privileged to share with the man I call boss – one who has been to me a father, mentor, benefactor, teacher, and, above all, a blessing from God Almighty. April 21, 2004, marked the beginning of a journey that would forever alter the course of my life. As I approached the wine-coloured plywood door on the second floor of a six-storey building at Ijora Causeway, Lagos – then the headquarters of The Comet newspaper – I opened it and found myself face to face with Mr. Omotoso, the Daily Editor, who needed someone to run errands for his office. He asked my name. “Robert,” I replied. “When will you resume work?” he asked. I was stunned. nigeria.description: The United Nations General Assembly has, for the first time, formally endorsed a global shift away from the centuries-old Mercator map in favour of projections that show Africa—and other equatorial regions—in their true relative size. This “Correct the Map” resolution, spearheaded by Togo on behalf of the African Group and backed by the African Union, passed by 164 votes to one, with six abstentions. While non-binding, it marks a watershed moment in how the world visually represents the continent—and, by extension, how it perceives Africa’s weight in global affairs. The root of the misrepresentation lies in the Mercator projection, devised in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator for maritime navigation. To keep compass bearings straight, Mercator preserved angles and shapes—but at the cost of area. The result: landmasses near the poles, such as Europe, North America and Greenland, are visually enlarged, while those near the equator, including Africa, Latin America and South Asia, are shrunk. On typical Mercator wall maps, Greenland appears roughly the same size as Africa. In reality, Africa covers about 30.3 million square kilometres, making it around 14 times larger than Greenland’s 2.1 million square kilometres. This is not a minor quirk; it is a systematic visual bias baked into the most widely used world map for nearly five centuries. The resolution encourages governments, schools, international organisations, media houses and technology companies to adopt equal-area projections, especially the Equal Earth projection, whenever comparative continental size matters. It frames map distortion as more than a technical issue—calling it a cognitive, educational, cultural and geopolitical problem that has contributed to the symbolic minimisation of Africa in the global imagination. While symbolic correction matters, Africa’s greatest vulnerabilities lie in structural exploitation and escalating insecurity, notably from Islamist insurgencies across the Sahel, Lake Chad Basin and parts of the Horn. Map reform must be paired with hard-edged action on multiple fronts. nigeria.description: Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said Wednesday he is optimistic Barcelona winger Lamine Yamal will be fit to face England in the Nations League at the weekend. The 19-year-old winger will miss the world champions’ visit to face the Czech Republic in Prague on Thursday with a knee problem and is set to join up with Spain after that game. Yamal played for Barcelona in the 2-1 La Liga win over Atletico Madrid on Sunday and on Monday Spain said he would not travel to face the Czechs. “He got hurt in the last match, he had some discomfort in one knee, he went for the usual treatment, a scan in Barcelona, and they saw he had inflammation and fluid in the knee — that meant he needed rest,” De la Fuente told reporters. “Our medical staff and his medical staff have a fantastic relationship, and I decided that his trip here should be avoided without knowing whether he’d be in any condition to play.” The coach said he had spoken to the winger and his recovery was looking positive ahead of England’s visit to Madrid on Sunday. “He’s doing a series of exercises with his physio and with the club that indicate the recovery is going well,” continued De la Fuente. “We believe, I’m optimistic, that on Friday he’ll be with us.” De la Fuente dismissed the idea that Yamal, who came third in the Ballon d’Or voting in October, has any special privileges compared to his La Roja team-mates. “He has no privileges, and his team-mates are relaxed about it, because we treat everyone the same,” added the coach. “In similar situations we would have done exactly the same for any other player, and the players know that.” – Unstoppable run – Spain have won all four games so far in Group A3 and sealed qualification to the quarter-finals. De la Fuente’s side are unbeaten in their last 43 competitive outings, and the coach said it provided his team with extra motivation. “We want to keep setting new milestones, and this is another one,” explained De la Fuente. “None of us would probably ever have thought we’d even reach 35, because we already felt those were astronomical numbers, but having reached 43, you think, my goodness, we want to get to 44, of course we do.” Spain won their previous outing away in Croatia with a brace from Arsenal’s Mikel Merino. nigeria.description: The Canada government has announced plans to accelerate permanent residence (PR) processing for up to 200,000 foreign nationals already living in the country in 2027, as part of efforts to reduce immigration application backlogs and provide greater certainty for newcomers. The initiative, announced by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) under the 2027–2029 Immigration Levels Plan, will provide additional admissions spaces for selected workers and humanitarian applicants seeking to transition to permanent residence. According to the government, the measure will be implemented through two major groups: a workers’ cohort and a humanitarian cohort, with up to 100,000 spaces allocated to each. The workers’ category will cover eligible foreign workers already living in Canada, alongside their accompanying family members. The government intends to work with provincial and territorial authorities to identify workers who meet regional labour market requirements. Eligible workers will include those who qualify for permanent residence through the Provincial Nominee Program (PNP), as well as applicants awaiting decisions under selected federal immigration programmes. These programmes include the Atlantic Immigration Program, Start-Up Visa Program, Self-Employed Persons Program, Agri-Food Pilot and Home Care Worker programmes. The humanitarian category, also allocated up to 100,000 spaces, will cover people already in Canada who have been waiting for permanent residence decisions, including applicants under specific family reunification and humanitarian pathways. Among those expected to benefit from the humanitarian allocation are: Spouses, common-law partners and dependent children: Family members of Canadian citizens and permanent residents who have already applied for permanent residence and are awaiting final decisions. Hong Kong residents: Applicants under Canada’s permanent residence pathways for Hong Kong residents, which closed to new applications on August 31, 2026. Ukrainian nationals: Applicants under the Ukraine Family Reunification Pathway, which closed to new applications on October 22, 2024. Humanitarian and compassionate applicants: Individuals already in Canada whose applications for permanent residence have received approval in principle. The government said the additional spaces would help it process all remaining applications under the Hong Kong and Ukraine pathways, while also supporting family reunification and fulfilling existing humanitarian commitments. IRCC also said the initiative would help reduce waiting periods for spouses and partners of Canadian citizens and permanent residents, with the aim of bringing processing times closer to 12 months for applicants destined for provinces outside Quebec. nigeria.title: US withdraws from U17 World Cup in Qatar over security fears
nigeria.description: The United States has withdrawn from the upcoming Under-17 soccer World Cup in Qatar due to concerns about security in the Middle East, US media reported Wednesday. Players were informed of the decision just over a week before the tournament is due to begin on November 19, US Soccer Collective and The Athletic reported, citing anonymous sources. US Soccer, the sport’s governing body in the United States, did not immediately confirm the news or respond to AFP’s request for comment. The war in the Middle East began in February with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which retaliated by targeting, among others, Gulf countries allied with Washington. Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have been punctuated by repeated threats from the United States and Israel to resume bombardments of Iran. Multiple sporting events in the Middle East have been affected, including the tennis WTA Finals which were scheduled to be held in Saudi Arabia — which neighbors Qatar — but are instead now taking place at Indian Wells in the US. This season’s Formula One Grand Prix in Jeddah was cancelled, while the race in Bahrain was called off and later rescheduled under the same name in Malaysia. Several events in Saudi Arabia have also been cancelled or postponed in recent weeks following attacks on the country by the Houthis in Yemen. The US is one of 48 teams scheduled to play in the Under-17 World Cup, in a group with Montenegro, Chile and Algeria. The Under-17 World Cup shifted to an annual event last year, and is being held in Qatar for five consecutive years. Announcing its host decision in 2024, FIFA said the decision to choose a single host nation for multiple editions centered on the ability to make “use of existing footballing infrastructure in the interest of tournament efficiencies and sustainability”. The decision is part of MSCI’s November 2026 Index Review , posted shortly after 5 p.m. ET. Official additions and deletions lists show Strategy (MSTR) out of its USA Index, which also takes it out of the broader MSCI World and ACWI indexes. The same review deletes Japan’s Metaplanet from the MSCI Japan Small Cap Index and uranium holder Yellow Cake from the MSCI United Kingdom Small Cap Index, and it removes Iceland’s Skel Fjárfestingafélag from the MSCI Iceland Frontier Markets Small Cap Index and micro-cap Upexi from the USA Micro Cap Index. All five had already been marked Deleted on MSCI’s potential-impact list , built on Sept. 30 financial data and Oct. 9 market values. Strategy is the only large-cap name in the group and, on that October list, accounted for more than 90% of the five companies’ combined float-adjusted market value. Strategy shares closed at $122.35, up 1.06%, then slipped 1.51% to $120.50 in after-hours trading as of 5:34 p.m. ET. How the MSCI screen works The rule does not mention bitcoin. The index first checks whether a company’s operating assets equal at least 50% of total assets. Issuers that fail that core screen face five financial ratios, and a company flagged on four or more of them is ineligible for the MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes. Buffers limit turnover. A company outside the indexes cannot be added if it fails the ineligibility screen in either of its two most recent annual filing periods, but a current constituent is removed only if it fails in each of them. The index said it may also use the most recent interim filing. MSCI also said Wednesday that the same non-operating treatment will apply to the MSCI US Index Series. The screen replaces an approach aimed squarely at crypto. The index first proposed in late 2025 to exclude companies whose digital assets made up 50% or more of total assets, then dropped that plan in January and opened a broader consultation in August. It adopted the new methodology on Oct. 15, with minor modifications, and said it would end the interim measures it had placed on those companies in October 2025, including a freeze on share-count increases and a deferral of additions. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, communicate and solve problems. In today’s world, if you’re not on board with AI, it could be said you’re being resistant to the fastest-growing technological innovation in the world. From students researching academic subjects to professionals developing business ideas, AI tools have become companions in everyday activities for people. They can help save time, explore new ideas, understand difficult concepts and approach tasks differently. However, as more people embrace these AI tools, it is important to understand that using AI effectively goes beyond knowing what prompts to enter. It requires knowing when to use it, how to question its responses and, most importantly, when to rely on your own knowledge and judgement. AI could make us better at what we do, not make us dependent on it. Here are ways we think you use AI effectively: Use AI as a Research Assistant One of the most effective ways to use AI is for research and information gathering. Whether you are writing an article, preparing a presentation or exploring an unfamiliar subject, AI can help you identify relevant topics, explain complex ideas and suggest areas worth investigating. You can ask it to break down unfamiliar concepts, identify key questions, or suggest research directions. However, do not treat every response as fact. Verify important information using credible sources, published research, books and reliable websites. AI can help you find information, but you are responsible for establishing what is true. Use AI to Brainstorm and Explore Ideas Like knowledge gathering, AI can brainstorm ideas with you. Sometimes, the hardest part of starting a project is knowing where to begin. AI can help you overcome this challenge by suggesting ideas, exploring different approaches and presenting perspectives you may not have considered. For writers, entrepreneurs, researchers and creatives, it can be a useful brainstorming partner. You can share an idea, ask questions about its strengths and weaknesses, and explore ways to develop it. However, brainstorming should not become an excuse to surrender your imagination. entertainment.title: How Heineken Created Immersive Experiences That Took Lagos Fashion Week 2026 Beyond the Runway
entertainment.description: In a city where creativity is a culture and every corner has a story to tell, Heineken brought another expression of Lagos to life at Lagos Fashion Week 2026 . Through its City of Cities: Where Taste Rules experience, the brand transformed its eleven-year partnership with the fashion showcase into a celebration of the people, ideas, and experiences shaping the city’s creative identity, bringing fashion, music, innovation, and social connections together across the week. From runway presentations to the Heineken Lounge, the debut of Heineken Studio, and an energetic after-party, the brand created experiences that went beyond the collections on display, inviting guests to explore new expressions of taste, discover creative possibilities, and connect over shared interests. At the heart of the experience was City of Cities: Where Taste Rules, an experience inspired by the many influences that make Lagos what it is. First introduced in 2025, the concept recognises that Lagos is more than one city; it is a melting pot of different cultures, communities, sounds, and styles. At Lagos Fashion Week 2026, Heineken brought this idea into focus, celebrating the diversity of expression that makes the city’s creative scene distinct. The experience also marked another chapter in Heineken’s eleven-year journey with Lagos Fashion Week. Over the years, the partnership has explored the intersection of fashion, craftsmanship, and taste through initiatives such as Woven Threads in 2022, the Dyelab collaboration in 2023, and the H45 Collection in 2024, before introducing City of Cities: Where Taste Rules in 2025. Each edition has created a new way to engage with fashion and culture, with this year’s experience building on that foundation through fresh expressions of creativity and innovation. Aligned with the 2026 theme, CRAFTED: Heritage. Innovation. Circular Futures, Heineken’s presence celebrated the artistry, intentionality, and evolving perspectives shaping contemporary fashion. Across the venue, guests arrived in style, adding their own interpretations of fashion and self-expression to the atmosphere. The Heineken Lounge provided a space to unwind, exchange ideas, and connect as guests enjoyed chilled Heineken, refreshments, and the runway presentations. The experience also offered a taste of something different, with guests exploring Foam Infusions in exciting variations, including espresso and blood orange. A major highlight was the Nigerian debut of Heineken Studio, the brand’s Playground of Innovation, which brought together taste, creativity, and personal expression in an interactive space. Beyond discovering new ways to experience lager through Foam Infusions, guests could step into the painting studio to create personalised designs on their own Heineken cans. The photo area and Heineken-branded backdrops also became popular spots for guests to capture their moments, express their individual styles, and share their experiences. sports.title: Rutgers women's basketball wins but major scare from Monmouth, Gigi Gamble
sports.description: PISCATAWAY -- The Rutgers women's basketball team avoided an upset Wednesday night when the Scarlet Knights came back from 17-point deficit to defeat Monmouth University 64-62. With the game tied 62-62, Mia Pauldo got the ball off the screen, drove right, stopped and hit a midrange jumper to give Rutgers the lead with 3.4 seconds left. The possession before, Pauldo hit a floater in the paint to get the lead before Monmouth's Gigi Gamble tied it up with free throws. More: Rutgers women's basketball has Hope. Masonius comes home for new beginning | Exclusive Monmouth led by as much as 17 points but the game was tied after Rutgers went on an 18-6 run in the third quarter. "Honestly, we had this game," said Monmouth's Gigi Gamble, who had a game-high 30 was named the Coastal Athletic Conference Preseason Player of the Year. "We had it, it hurts, but it should give us more fuel, more fight, more hunger, more heart." "We're going to keep building off it. So I'm not worried about this loss." Rutgers is 4-0 but this was by far the closest call the Big Ten team has had. "Coach (Gary Redus) had a talk while I was on the bench and he said the best players aren't who they are when things are only going good for them, they're who they are when things are going bad for them," said Pauldo, who scored 7 points in the first half but finished with a team-high 17. "I took that in and was like, yeah I want to be the best player and I was messing up in the first half and I wasn't focused enough. And I was like to take responsibility in this game, if we really want to win this game I got to lock in and step up and be the best player." Monmouth got a chance to tie with 3.0 seconds left but turned the ball over on the inbounds to seal the win for the Scarlet Knights. The Scarlet Knights (4-0) came out the gate slow but picked up the defensive pressure in the second half to hold off a Monmouth (2-1) team that's projected to win the Coastal Athletic Association Conference. So far this season, Rutgers has faced mid-majors and Tuesday was no different, but the level of pressure was different. Redus labeled the game a "wake up call." "I would've liked us to be a little bit more aggressive tonight," Redus said. "I felt like we could've come out and we could've had more aggression especially on the defensive end. I didn't like our defensive effort at all in the first half. That was the issue. We had nine points in the first quarter but the offense is gonna be hit or miss at times with any team. Especially in close games, it's your defense that has to carry you." They shot 55% in the first half so that's what I told them, it was the defense." One of the biggest bright spots for Rutgers was the way it was able share the ball. Eight different Scarlet Knights were able to score the ball on Wednesday which came in handy. Especially in the third quarter when Rutgers went on a 18-2 run to go into the last quarter tied 44-44. Rutgers first lead came with 9:28 left in the last quarter

sports.title: Ford Veterans Day Classic at Daytona is a hit. Will it return? If so, where?
sports.description: Yes, we can call it the “inaugural” Veterans Day Classic at Daytona. We’ll eventually see the TV numbers from USA Network’s Wednesday night coverage. But the eyeball test suggests a hit for the Ford Motor Company, its Ford Racing division, and the combo of NASCAR and Daytona International Speedway. “We love throwing races. We love throwing big events. We love partnering with friends like Ford,” Speedway President Frank Kelleher said Wednesday night while mixing in the thick FanZone crowd. Logistics can be, you know, logistical, and sometimes timing and schedules are a challenge, but Veterans Day appears to fall in a unique place on the calendar — right after the NASCAR season, just before the holidays start dominating the scene. Thankfully, Veterans Day isn’t going anywhere, and my guess is Ford will always have cars to sell, so maybe this becomes a yearly thing. “I would love it,” Kelleher said. “We know how to execute high-level music acts. Music and racing are definitely in our DNA.” Except he then tossed in a wrinkle worth noting. “We will be excited to chat with Ford and everyone involved in the weeks to come and see if it makes sense to bring it back, whether it be here at Daytona International Speedway or perhaps at another speedway.” Will Veterans Day Classic return? Probably. But where? … Or perhaps at another Speedway. That seems like a logical move. However, and back to logistics, Wednesday’s event had the advantage of blending into an existing Daytona race week — Historic Sportscar Racing’s 12th annual Daytona Classic 24, which started Wednesday and runs through Sunday. The track’s race operations were already in place, which brings a nice advantage. We’re LIVE from Daytona for the Veterans Day Classic! 🇺🇸🏁 📺 : USA Netwok pic.twitter.com/cZOeXCYmIm — NASCAR on USA (@NASCARonUSA) November 12, 2026 Given the HSR presence, the garage area was wall-to-wall with a wide variety of yesterday’s racing machinery, including cars that previously ran here in both stock-car and sportscar races. For anyone who walked the grounds and saw the recent racing equipment and virtual museum pieces, there was contrast, since one of two threads running through it all was promotion of Ford’s new Mustang Dark Horse. The NASCAR version of the new Mustang was unveiled Wednesday afternoon at the museum outside Turn 4. The road-racing version was center stage for the 30-minute race on Daytona’s Rolex 24 road course. The other thread, of course, was Veterans Day. The Speedway and NASCAR have always leaned heavily toward the promotion of our nation’s military and its veterans. Usually, it’s part of the show. Wednesday, that theme blanketed the entire evening of loud music and louder machines. And you’d have a hard time finding anything other than a thumbs-up from those who joined the festivities. sports.title: Revived Fuellkrug relishes home comforts on Germany return
sports.description: Niclas Fuellkrug (R) has been in top form since returning to Werder Bremen (Kirill KUDRYAVTSEV) After ill-fated stints at West Ham and AC Milan, striker Niclas Fuellkrug's rich vein of form since his Werder Bremen return has been capped with a Germany recall. Germany coach Jurgen Klopp brought Fuellkrug back into the fold for Nations League fixtures against Serbia on Friday and the Netherlands next week. Fuellkrug has not played an international game since a Nations League third-place playoff loss to France in June 2025. While Klopp, who has a contract until after the 2030 World Cup, has stated his focus is on youth and building for the future, Fuellkrug made himself impossible to ignore. Currently the Bundesliga's top scorer ahead of Harry Kane, the 33-year-old has 12 goals in 11 matches in all competitions, having managed only four in two seasons after leaving Germany for West Ham. Klopp admitted "sometimes form trumps everything else". "He made his case with a wide variety of goals... and almost all of them were spectacular," said Klopp. Fuellkrug also has an excellent record for Germany with 14 goals in just 24 appearances, many of which came as a substitute. Fuellkrug has a simple explanation for his form since returning to Bremen on a season-long loan from now-Championship side West Ham. "It's my footballing home," Fuellkrug said of the club he first joined aged 14. "Everyone sleeps better in their own bed. I just feel completely at ease here." Fuellkrug became the latest striker to endure an unhappy time at West Ham, a club which has become a graveyard for promising European forwards. He scored just three times in an injury-hit 18 months in London. But while he may not have gotten among the goals, his endeared himself to some of the fanbase with his typically German honesty. After conceding late to draw 1-1 at home to Southampton in April 2025, Fuellkrug spoke his mind, using a swear word to describe the Hammers' performance, with the West Ham fans then using his quote to create a chant referencing him. Fuellkrug's honesty has also won him support among many in Germany, where the gap-toothed journeyman is seen as an antidote to the modern image-conscious footballer. "I couldn't stay fit," Fuellkrug said of his struggles abroad, adding: "The key is staying fit and having a team around me that looks for me -- and passes me the ball when the moment is right. "That's the key -- I think I've been able to prove that now." - Klose an 'inspiration' - Fuellkrug is in blistering form but his call-up highlights how bare the cupboard now is in a country once known for producing top-class forwards. The four-time world champions have produced strikers like Gerd Mueller, Fritz Walter, Ulf Kirsten, Rudi Voeller and Jurgen Klinsmann. But Germany have not had a top-class number nine since 2014 World Cup-winner Miroslav Klose. Of Germany's current generation, Kai Havertz regularly starts up front but the Arsenal man has never been an out-and-out goalscorer.

Get back on the winning track, especially get in front of our home fans. That’s the ultimate focus, is focus on that. All the outside things, going against my former team, that stuff was in the past. Four, five years ago? Yeah, it was a big deal,” Watson said. “Now, I think both sides have moved on, and we’re just both trying to find ways to win and continue to put ourselves in position for later on down the road.” Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans also had plenty of praise for Watson, highlighting his decision-making and ability to escape pressure. “I’ve seen a guy who’s being very decisive with the football. He’s getting the ball out of his hands very quickly. When it’s not there, it’s his athletic ability to escape the pocket,” Ryans said. The attack, which Ukrainian press said was ordered by Kyiv, happened in early October and caused a fire and subsequent outage at Yandex’s ru-central1-b availability zone. On Tuesday, Yandex posted an update on its recovery efforts, which it spun as something of a triumph because it restored over 97 percent of customer data. Of course that also means the company lost 2.84 percent of customer data, which it blamed on “critical hardware damage and a lack of backups on the platform.” It’s unclear if Yandex’s use of the phrase “on the platform” indicates it doesn’t keep backups of its own cloud, if whatever resilience techniques it employs don’t create multiple copies of customer data, or if clients didn’t protect their data. Whatever happened, Yandex has decided to enable backups by default for all VMs customers create in its cloud. That decision will mean customers will consume and pay for more Yandex resources, unless they opt out of the automated backups. Given that drones damaged three Yandex locations, and the war with Ukraine continues, users have good reasons to consider alternatives to its services. Indeed, Yandex’s announcement of its recovery efforts links to a page extolling the virtues of a hybrid cloud when devising data protection strategies. That page also mentions Yandex’s own Stackland product, which brings its stack on-prem, as an example of a hybrid approach. On Wednesday the company also launched a new availability zone named ru-central1-f. Yandex didn’t say where it’s located, other than to say it’s in “a new location.” Interestingly, Yandex has imposed quotas that limit the amount of resources users can access in the new availability zone and says it can’t yet handle traffic to private endpoints at the new facility. Many nations have imposed sanctions that restrict sales of technology products to Russia. It’s therefore unsurprising that Yandex might struggle to provision enough infrastructure to allow untrammeled access to a new availability zone. ®

technology.title: US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity
technology.description: Datacenter power consumption in the US is growing roughly ten times faster than grid capacity, meaning facilities may soon need to find a large chunk of their own electricity from other sources. Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it's needed. Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing. Gartner warned in June that the energy consumed by AI datacenters is on track to grow 26 percent this year, and grid supply may be unable to keep pace with demand by the end of this decade. Howden's analysis of data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and S&P Global found that since the year 2000, power being fed to data campuses has risen 19 percent a year on average, while the electricity grid expanded capacity by just 2 percent per annum over the same period. Datacenters' share of US grid capacity was circa five percent in 2025, up from 0.1 percent in 2000 – a 50-fold increase. Management consultancy Bain & Company issued a report two years ago warning that energy companies must switch gear and invest in building out grid capacity faster , as energy draw by server farms is expected to more than double by 2030. This doesn't mean that datacenters are in danger of eating all of America's electricity, at least not in the immediate future. The graph makes it appear that the two lines are about to cross, but the chart uses different scales: 1,400 gigawatts on the left axis for grid capacity, versus just 80 on the right for datacenters. Keeping datacenters at five percent of grid capacity requires 110 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity by 2030, Howden estimates – an expansion it considers unlikely. Instead, it expects a combination of greater reliance on the grid, slower development at power-constrained sites, and alternative supplies. For the largest, most power-constrained projects, Howden warns that grid delays of two to six years could mean $800 million to $2.4 billion in forgone revenue. "Power availability is becoming one of the defining challenges of the datacenter boom," says Howden head of Natural Resources Stuart Adam. "As demand for AI infrastructure accelerates, developers are increasingly looking beyond traditional grid connections to secure the electricity they need." Howden's business is insurance, and so Adam also notes that on-site generation introduces new operational and financial exposures, as operators take greater responsibility for their power infrastructure. ®

The finding adds to a mixed story for the power of global restrictions. The levels of perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in English rivers have fallen by 30 per cent and 29 per cent, respectively, over the past decade, according to a new report by scientists at the Environment Agency (EA) , a UK government green regulator. Both of these human-made chemicals take a long time to break down in the environment. Here's the PSRA strategy: Develop impartial recommendations for retrieving the Martian samples collected by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover and deliver them to Earth Assess proposed mission requirements Review prior lessons learned Evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028. science.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
science.description:
Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. 

Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound. Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star. Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources. As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now. "Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them. The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling. The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website , the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old. Each burst arrives with its high frequencies first and sweeps downward, stretched by its journey through intergalactic gas, "and you can hear that dispersion as it falls from the dome," Melchior told Space.com by email. science.description: null On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon. Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin . NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks. Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day. The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program . Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11 , and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13 . The Gemini 12 astronauts James Lovell and Edwin Aldrin lifted off aboard a Titan launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center on November 11, 1966, an hour and a half after their Agena target vehicle was orbited by an Atlas rocket. (Image credit: NASA/MSFC) Why it mattered Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon. It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11. "This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview . "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station . As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water." science.title: Blood-thinning drug limits cartilage damage and relieves osteoarthritis pain
science.description: Coloured X-ray of osteoarthritis of the knee ALAIN POL/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY A drug that prevents blood clots reduced pain and improved mobility in mice and monkeys with knee osteoarthritis. The approach seems to partly work by reducing inflammatory signals that degrade cartilage. Osteoarthritis is caused by the wear and tear of cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, leading to inflammation, pain and stiffness. It affects more than 500 million people worldwide. Painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs can relieve symptoms, but no approved drugs halt or slow worsening of the disease. “We have nothing to offer our patients apart from suggesting weight loss, or offering drugs that provide pain relief,” says Tonia Vincent at the University of Oxford, who wasn’t involved in the study. Advertisement Read more The best non-drug therapies to relieve the pain of knee osteoarthritis It is widely thought that inflammatory molecules called TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta drive inflammation that worsens osteoarthritis. This has led to clinical trials testing drugs that target either of these molecules. But these have been unsuccessful, potentially because these molecules compensate for each other when one is blocked, according to Chuan-Ju Liu at Yale University and his colleagues. To explore whether targeting both molecules may be more effective, the researchers surgically removed part of the cartilage in the left knee joints of eight monkeys to mimic wear and tear that triggers osteoarthritis. A month later, four of the monkeys took a daily dose of a drug called dabigatran, mixed into their food. Dabigatran is commonly used to prevent blood clots in people at increased risk of strokes, but has also been shown to block inflammatory signals via both TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta. The remaining monkeys ate their usual food as a control. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter After seven months, MRI scans revealed that the left-knee cartilage in monkeys on dabigratan was about 60 per cent thicker, on average, compared to the control monkeys. This suggests that the drug reduced cartilage damage, slowing the progression of osteoarthritis, says Liu. Monkeys on dabigratan also had a roughly 15 per cent greater range of motion in their left knee than the control monkeys. “Monkeys receiving dabigatran showed a more natural walking pattern and a greater range of knee movement,” says Liu. “These improvements are consistent with reduced joint stiffness and discomfort.” In further experiments, the team confirmed their findings in mice with surgically-induced knee osteoarthritis, which also revealed that dabigratan reduced inflammation in the knee by about 60 per cent. science.title: Andy Weir's 'Exoplanet' just landed on Audible, but what actually makes an exoplanet habitable?
science.description: null Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead. This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo . Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable? Learning from the stars An artist's concept illustrates a young, red dwarf star surrounded by three planets. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock. For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it. Using a technique called spectroscopy , astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance. Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere. A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise. Hostile stars Black holes are bad news for life, but living stars provide just as many problems. (Image credit: Audible) A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere . Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star. science.title: Who will step up to preserve space age artefacts for future generations?
science.description: NASA/JPL-Caltech Around 40,000 years from now, the Voyager 1 probe will pass within astronomical spitting distance of the star Gliese 445. From there, it will continue drifting through the universe on an endless journey that marks humanity’s first attempt to reach the stars. Voyager 1 – which on 18 November will have travelled one light day from Earth – began its odyssey almost 50 years ago, meaning it has been operating for the majority of the space age. That makes it a rarity: most of our iconic spacecraft ended their lives burned up in Earth’s atmosphere or in bits at the bottom of the ocean. Two of the most important missions still flying today, the Hubble Space Telescope and the International Space Station, look set to share the same fate in the near future, even as scientists call for Hubble to be preserved . While some craft like the space shuttles are on display in museums, our present space history is, essentially, in its dark ages, with little thought currently given to preserving spacecraft in situ, where our space-travelling descendants may wish to marvel at them. Even the Apollo hardware left behind on the moon has almost no protection in international law. Advertisement Perhaps we need an organisation like the UNESCO World Heritage Committee to designate important space artefacts for preservation, and encourage funding from cultural and heritage budgets, not scientific ones, to do this. Of course, with such budgets often under threat and the US set to leave UNESCO at the end of this year, this could introduce new problems. Private philanthropy is another option. If humanity is to one day take its place among the stars, a fantasy that fuels many a tech billionaire, it would be a great shame to not be able to look back at how we got there. Just as we remember 19th-century captains of industry like Andrew Carnegie and J. P. Morgan for funding great cultural institutions, perhaps we should be lobbying for the creation of a Musk Space Museum or Bezos Orbital Institute.

Shot by Roger Patterson and Robert Gimlin in 1967, the clip became one of the canonical pieces of evidence for the existence of Bigfoot: a mythical humanoid that supposedly lives in the forests of North America. Bigfoot is one of the icons of cryptozoology, the search for probably-nonexistent creatures. It has hordes of devotees. science.title: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
science.description: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space? New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth. "Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement . Stripping the romance from the Earth's turbulent past Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system ’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets. For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely. Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves. In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS . An artist’s impression of a comet crashing into the early Earth (Image credit: Scarlett White) The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second). Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry. science.title: 'There's tremendous demand': Rocket Lab raises price of Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million
science.description: null The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground. Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027. "Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher." Rocket Lab is best known for Electron , a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO). Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO. Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control). Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30. The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. Neutron's first 16 launches are now sold out, he added, and bookings from here on will be for flights in the 2030s. "The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck," Beck said. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) That bottleneck is coming in 2028 or so, when SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 rocket .
